name: Hubble's Law & Cosmic Expansion
kick: gravity & geometry · first principles · space itself stretches
title: Recession by the meter — why distant galaxies rush away faster, without any center
lede: Nearly every galaxy we see is moving away from us — and the farther it is, the faster it recedes. If every galaxy is running away, doesn't that mean we are at the center of some cosmic explosion? No. The trick is that space itself is stretching everywhere at once, like the dough in rising raisin bread. The Hubble rate tells us how fast. Here is the problem that sparked the reframe, the measured numbers that reveal the law, why there is no special center, what breaks the simple picture, and the cosmic surprise it led to.
arc: Why no center: space stretches uniformly

sections.h2: 1 · The problem — every galaxy is running away from us, faster if farther

blocks.html: Astronomers measure how fast distant galaxies move by looking at their light. Nearby galaxies scatter in random directions — some toward us, some away. But once you look far enough out, a strange pattern appears: every distant galaxy is receding — moving away. Stranger still: the farther the galaxy, the faster it goes. A galaxy twice as far is receding twice as fast. A galaxy ten times farther is receding ten times as fast. A clean, straight-line relationship.

The stakes are immediate: if everything is running away from us, does that mean Earth is at the center of the cosmos? That would overturn five hundred years of learning that we are not special. So this is not idle wonder — it is a crisis demanding an answer.

sections.h2: 2 · The reframe — space itself expands; we are not at any center

blocks.html: The reframe throws out the idea that galaxies are moving through static space. Instead, space itself is stretching. Imagine a loaf of raisin bread rising in the oven. The raisins are galaxies. As the dough expands, every raisin sees all the others moving away — faster if farther — purely because the dough between them is getting bigger. A raisin halfway across the loaf sees the expansion pushing it back at half the speed of a raisin all the way across. There is no special center, no explosion point. The dough stretches everywhere equally, and every raisin sees the same cosmic pattern.

The Hubble rate is the speed at which the dough (space) is rising — how many kilometers per second the universe adds per megaparsec of separation. Measure that one number, and you have a ruler for the entire cosmic expansion.

sections.h2: 3 · Seen on a real run — recession speed rises in step with distance

blocks.html: We computed the recession speeds of galaxies at three distances using a Hubble rate of 70 kilometers per second per megaparsec — the rate from direct cosmic measurements. Every number here is that computation.

blocks.caption: A megaparsec is about 3.3 million light-years. A redshift of z ~ 0.002 means the light's wavelength stretches by 0.2% during its journey.

blocks.html: The discovered fact: recession speed climbs in exact proportion to distance — 700 km/s at 10 Mpc, 7,000 at 100 Mpc, 70,000 at 1,000 Mpc. It is a perfect straight line, Hubble's law. This is the signature of space expanding uniformly everywhere. Only a uniform stretching of the dough gives a speed exactly proportional to the distance between raisins — and it looks identical no matter which raisin you are standing on.

sections.h2: 4 · Why no center: space stretches uniformly, so every galaxy sees the same pattern

blocks.html: The key is the word "uniformly." If one region of space were inflating faster than another, then galaxies in the slow zone would feel pulled away from the fast zone — that is, a center would emerge. But measurements show the expansion is the same in every direction and at every location. A galaxy 10 Mpc away sees us receding at 700 km/s just as it sees another galaxy 10 Mpc away receding at 700 km/s in its own direction.

This is the scale-factor picture: imagine attaching an invisible grid to space. As space expands, the grid expands with it, stretching every ruler and every distance by the same factor each second. If you live on a raisin and measure distances to nearby raisins, they grow by exactly that factor. You see all your neighbors receding at speeds proportional to their distance from you. A raisin on the other side of the loaf sees the same thing — its neighbors all receding proportionally. There is no unique center because the expansion is the same everywhere.

sections.h2: 5 · The one real limit — nearby galaxies muddy the pattern, and the expansion rate changes over time

blocks.html: The Hubble law works cleanly only for distant galaxies. Galaxies nearby — within a few hundred million light-years — have their own individual motions superimposed on the cosmic expansion. The Andromeda galaxy is actually moving toward us, not away, because gravity has bound it into our local group. The jitter obscures the simple linear relationship until you step back and look far.

Worse, the expansion rate itself has changed over cosmic history. The universe expanded fast after the Big Bang, then slowed down as gravity tugged galaxies together. But about six billion years ago, the expansion began to speed up — a shock that forced physicists to invent "dark energy." So the Hubble number 70 km/s per megaparsec is only today's snapshot. Measure galaxies from billions of years ago, and you get a different number. The law is local in time as well as in the scale range where you measure it.

sections.h2: 6 · The surprise — run the expansion backward and you reach a hot, dense beginning

blocks.html: If space is stretching now, what was it doing in the past? Run the movie backward: the universe was denser yesterday than today, denser the day before, and so on. Extrapolate to the limit and you reach a state of infinite density at a finite time in the past — the moment that would later be called the Big Bang. The Hubble rate is the expansion speed now; if you know that and you know the mass-energy budget, you can compute how long ago all the matter was squeezed into a point. The age of the universe emerges directly from a simple measurement of how fast galaxies recede.

The Hubble law was discovered in the 1920s; by the 1950s it drove cosmology toward the idea of a hot beginning. Today, the acceleration of the expansion reveals the existence of dark energy, the dominant component of the universe. All from a straight-line plot of speed versus distance.

recipe.summary: Compute recession speeds at three distances using the Hubble rate (70 km/s per megaparsec) and the relation speed = Hubble rate × distance. Convert recession speed to redshift using z ≈ v/c for z < 0.3. numpy, SI units.
recipe.eq:
Hubble's law:  v = H₀ × d
v = recession speed (km/s)
H₀ = Hubble rate = 70 km/s/Mpc
d = distance (megaparsec)
redshift (low-speed approx):  z ≈ v/c  where c = 300,000 km/s
recipe.note: Full script: scripts/experiments/gr_run.py (EXP8). Numbers are the run's output verbatim. Hubble rate measured from Type Ia supernovae and cosmic microwave background; redshift-distance relation from direct spectroscopy.
